---
title: "Assessment workflow"
format: html
---

The five workflows divide historical climate characterization, model construction, projection analysis, weather generation, and simulation.
Their usual execution order is WF0 → WF1 → WF2 → WF3 → WF4, but this order is not a chain of scientific inputs.
WF1 and WF3 are independent prerequisites for WF4.
WF2 supplies context for interpreting the stress test; it does not supply its forcing.

| Stage | Scientific question | Main product |
|---|---|---|
| WF0 `analyze_climate` | What does the historical climate record say, and which forcing source should be used? | Source-specific climatology and, when multiple sources are supplied, comparison products |
| WF1 `build_model` | How does the basin model respond to the selected historical forcing? | Delineated basin, Wflow-SBM model, historical simulation, and optional observation-based evaluation |
| WF2 `analyze_projections` | Where do projected temperature and precipitation changes fall relative to the stress-test domain? | CMIP6 change factors by model, scenario, and horizon |
| WF3 `generate_scenarios` | What climate conditions and natural variability should be tested? | Retained collection of stochastic, perturbed weather series |
| WF4 `simulate_system` | How do selected hydrological indicators respond across those conditions? | Retained Wflow responses and immutable metric sets |

## Historical reference and model setup

WF0 is optional and does not require a hydrological model.
Use it alone when comparing candidate forcing sources before choosing one for the project.
WF1 delineates the basin, builds the distributed model from spatial data, runs the historical period, and can compare simulated variables with observations supplied at output locations.
Because the toolbox does not perform local calibration, the forcing and spatial source choices deserve explicit scrutiny.

## Projection context and stress-test experiment

WF2 summarizes changes in CMIP6 precipitation and temperature between a reference window and named future windows.
Those change factors are a **plausibility overlay** on the climate response surface.
WF3 instead conditions the stochastic weather generator on the selected historical climate source, creates realizations, and applies the configured temperature–precipitation perturbation grid.
The generated series form a durable collection that can be used by more than one simulation experiment.

WF4 runs Wflow-SBM for explicit runs from a ready collection and derives requested indicators from the retained responses.
It can also calculate a new metric set from completed responses without repeating model simulations.
Read [Models and methods](../scientific-approach/models-and-methods.qmd) for the scientific operations, and [Reading the outputs](../guide/outputs.qmd) for the product layout and joins.
